title: Hazel and the Will
premise: Coroner Hazel Crane receives a confession letter for the drowning death of Tobias Wren — postmarked the day after his funeral three years ago — claiming the death was no accident and pointing to a will that was never filed. As the statute of limitations looms, Hazel discovers Tobias's estate was quietly redirected through forged signatures, implicating the town's most respected families. Her investigation unearths a chain of complicity stretching from the church to the county clerk, and forces her to confront her own father's role as the original coroner who ruled the death accidental. In the end, Hazel files the amended report, the true heir inherits, and she buries her father's reputation beside the truth he drowned to protect.
about_author: R. M. Fairweather is the pen name of a former rural court clerk who spent a decade filing probate records in small-town Ohio. Their fiction is known for its quiet dread and its fascination with paper trails.

chapters.title: Postmarked the Day After
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Three years after ruling Tobias Wren's drowning accidental, Hazel receives an anonymous confession letter timed impossibly to his funeral's anniversary. The letter names no killer, only a will. She rereads her father's old autopsy notes and finds a page missing. Beat: unease disguised as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Walking the cemetery to clear her head, Hazel visits Tobias's grave and notices fresh flowers from someone who shouldn't care — his estranged sister, Vivian, who contested nothing and vanished after the funeral. Emotional beat: the weight of being the town's keeper of endings.

chapters.title: The Sister Who Signed Nothing
chapters.summary: Vivian's POV. In a motel two counties over, Vivian reveals she was never notified of probate; a signature she never wrote transferred Tobias's property to the Harrow Trust. She hands Hazel a photocopy of the forged document. Beat: guilt and fear of coming home.

chapters.title: Paper Doesn't Drown
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. At the county records office, Hazel traces the will's chain of custody and finds the clerk's stamp dated two days after Tobias's death — before the body was officially found. Someone knew. Beat: the first hard proof, and the first real fear.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: Deputy Marisol Vega's POV. Marisol, who pulled Tobias from the water, admits she saw a truck at the boat launch that night but was told to log it as a deer poacher. She's been carrying it three years. Beat: complicity as survival.

chapters.title: The Harrow Trust
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The trust's beneficiary is Councilman Aldous Harrow, Tobias's former business partner and the man who paid for the funeral. Hazel interviews him; his grief is flawless, his timeline airtight. Beat: the horror of a suspect who is also the town's benefactor.

chapters.title: Father's Files
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. In her late father's locked cabinet, Hazel finds the missing autopsy page: a contusion behind Tobias's ear, noted then struck through in her father's hand. Beat: grief curdling into betrayal.

chapters.title: Statute of Limitations
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel consults a disbarred lawyer, Ruth Okafor, who warns that the fraud claim dies in thirty-four days unless Hazel can produce the original will or a living witness. Beat: the clock starts, and Hazel commits.

chapters.title: The Confession's Second Letter
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. A second letter arrives, postmarked the day of the funeral, containing a key to a bus-station locker in Ashford. Inside: Tobias's handwritten will, naming Vivian sole heir — and accusing Harrow of the assault. Beat: hope with a hook in it.

chapters.title: Who Mails a Confession
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth analyzes the letters' typewriter font and paper, concluding they were written recently by someone with access to the funeral home's stationery. The confessor isn't confessing — they're directing. Beat: the mystery turns inward.

chapters.title: The Funeral Director's Hands
chapters.summary: Emmett Doyle, the funeral director, POV. Emmett confesses to Hazel that he mailed the letters on instructions from a sealed envelope Tobias left with him, to be opened 'if the town stays quiet too long.' Beat: a decent man who obeyed a dead man's spite.

chapters.title: Marisol's Report
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol reopens her incident log and names the truck: Harrow's, plates and all. Her chief orders her to stand down; she photocopies the page and gives it to Hazel instead. Beat: courage priced in a career.

chapters.title: Vivian Comes Home
chapters.summary: Vivian's POV. Vivian returns to town for the first time in three years and is met at the diner by Harrow, who offers her a settlement to sign away the estate. She records the conversation. Beat: fear transmuted into leverage.

chapters.title: The Contusion
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel quietly exumes the file photos and consults a forensic pathologist: the blow was pre-mortem, consistent with a struggle on the dock, not the water. Her father didn't just miss it — he buried it. Beat: the case becomes personal heresy.

chapters.title: Why My Father Lied
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel finds her father's unsent letter to the state board: Harrow's trust held the loan that kept the coroner's office funded, and her father traded the truth for the town's only morgue. Beat: the price of survival, made flesh.

chapters.title: Threats in Alphabetical Order
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel's office is ransacked; the will photocopy is taken but the locker key, hidden in a grave registry, is safe. A note on her desk: 'Some files stay closed.' Beat: dread at the doorstep.

chapters.title: Thirty Days
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth files the fraud petition with the will, Marisol's log, and Vivian's recording. Harrow's lawyer moves to suppress everything; the hearing is set for the statute's final week. Beat: the machinery of law grinding against the machinery of money.

chapters.title: The Night at the Boat Launch
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Following a tip, Hazel stakes out the dock and witnesses Harrow burning documents. Confronted, he admits the fight — Tobias threatened to expose the trust's embezzlement — but insists the river did the rest. Beat: the truth, half-confessed.

chapters.title: Hearing
chapters.summary: Vivian's POV. At the probate hearing, Harrow's counsel produces a 'recantation' from Emmett Doyle. Vivian takes the stand, plays the diner recording, and Marisol's log enters evidence over objection. Beat: testimony as combat.

chapters.title: What the Water Gave Back
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The judge voids the forged transfer, orders the estate to Vivian, and refers the assault to the state. Harrow, undone by the paper trail he thought he owned, is indicted. Beat: vindication that tastes like ash.

chapters.title: Amended Report
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel files an amended coroner's report — cause of death: blunt force trauma, manner: homicide — and attaches her father's struck-through page, unredacted. She tells the town the truth at the public record reading. Beat: grief and duty reconciled.

chapters.title: Every Name, Including Mine
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, epilogue. Hazel adds her father's complicity to the public record herself, then visits both graves — Tobias's and, in memory, her father's. The town keeps its distance; Vivian sends flowers. Beat: survival's price paid in full, and accepted.
